of renewable energies,[1–6] carbon dioxide sequestration and capture,[7–9] to electrochemical,[10–12] photo and photoelectrochemical techniques,[13–15] etc., have been explored to reduce carbon dioxide. These processes would be of particular interest if value-added products could be produced during the reduction of carbon dioxide. To date, researchers have identified various electrochemical metallic catalysts able to catalyze carbon dioxide into value-added products in aqueous and nonaqueous organic electrolytes. Product distribution has been found highly dependent on the catalysts and parameters used in electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide. For example, in aqueous electrolyte, In, Sn, Hg, Pb, and Bi catalysts are well known to yield HCOOH, while Au, Ag, and Zn catalysts have the capability to reduce carbon
dioxide to CO selectively, and Cu catalysts are found to produce higher percentage of hydrocarbon products.
As mentioned above, Hori et al.[16] reported that Cu is the only known metal capable of catalyzing the formation of great many kinds of hydrocarbon from carbon dioxide electroreduction, although an overpotential of more than 1 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) is required. A recent research by Jaramillo’s group[17] using the copper catalyst with a range of applied potentials observed a total of 16 different reaction products, and 12 of which were C2-C3 compounds. This observation further expanded people’s understanding to the possibility of CO2 electroreduction hydrocarbon products catalyzed by copper, including ketones, aldehydes, carboxylic acids, and alcohols. They claimed that the C2-C3 products might be formed via the dehydroxylation of the possible intermediates in their enol or diol form. Due to the large various possible products, great effort has been made in improving the selectivity of Cu-derived catalysts toward targeted products. Kanan’s group[18] showed that oxide-derived copper, which can be then reduced to form metallic copper, produced a mixture of CO and HCOOH from CO2 at moderate potentials with reasonable Faradaic efficiency (FE) toward CO (≈40% FE at 2.5 mA cm−2). Takanabe and coworkers[19–21] reported recently the postformation of Cu–In and Cu-–Sn alloys on the surface of oxide-derived copper. The asprepared materials exhibited high selectivity toward CO in CO2 reduction reactions: the Cu–In alloy exhibited an FE of 90% toward CO and a current density of −0.6 mA cm−2 at −0.5 V
The development of highly efficient, selective, and economic approaches for electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide to hydrocarbons is a promising way to promote the sustainable carbon cycle nowadays. Here, a stable cobaltdecorated copper catalyst is reported with significantly enhanced selectivity toward formic acid produced from CO2 through electrochemical reduction. This catalyst is prepared through the electrodeposition of cobalt on the surface of copper, followed by Ar and air atmosphere treatment. The as-prepared catalyst exhibits selective conversion of CO2 to formic acid with a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of ≈80% at an applied potential of −0.65 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode. Meanwhile, the copper electrode treated with the same conditions without cobalt decoration and the cobalt-decorated copper electrode without Ar treatment process only show an FE toward formic acid of ≈56% and ≈57% from CO2 reduction, respectively. This study represents a facile decoration method to prepare highly selective electrocatalysts for the efficient reduction of CO2 to value-added chemicals in aqueous electrolytes.

sections.heading: CO2 Reduction
sections.text:
The awareness of global warming caused by the emission of greenhouse gases has been rising in past decades, and great endeavor has been made in removal of carbon dioxide, which is the major composition of greenhouse gases, from environment. Therefore, research to optimize methods and catalysts for carbon dioxide conversion has been full of attractions. To date, a variety of strategies, ranging from increased utilization

© 2019 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim1900362 (2 of 7)
versus RHE, and the Cu–Sn alloy showed an FE greater than 90% toward CO and a current density of −1.0 mA cm−2 at −0.6 V versus RHE. Xie’s group[22] found that surface cobalt atoms of the atomically thin layers have higher intrinsic activity and selectivity toward formate production, at lower overpotentials, than do surface cobalt atoms on bulk samples. Partial oxidation of the atomic layers further increases their intrinsic activity, allowing stable current densities of about 10 mA cm−2 over 40 h, with ≈90% formate selectivity at an overpotential of only 0.24 V. Zhao et al.[23] reported the decoration of Cu electrode surface with phosphate ion, which can enhance the formic acid selectivity from CO2 reduction. Herein, we employed cobalt for the decoration of copper electrode. The Cu–Co samples were prepared systematically by varying deposition durations and then treated with Ar and air atmosphere and further reduced to form the oxide-derived cobalt decorated copper thin film catalysts. The results show that the as-prepared catalyst exhibits greatly improved selectivity (≈80% FE) toward formic acid at −0.65 V versus RHE, while the competitive H2 evolution can be greatly diminished.
The oxide-derived cobalt-decorated copper thin film catalyst was prepared and used as systematic characterization sample during the whole process to understand the surface information of the electrode. All potentials mentioned are versus RHE for simplicity and comparison, unless otherwise mentioned. Herein, the catalyst prepared under −0.25 V and deposited for 60 s followed by Ar atmosphere treatment at 650 °C for 2 h and air atmosphere treatment at 400 °C for 2 h was selected (marked as Cu-650-400 and CuCo-650-400), as shown in Scheme 1 and Figure S1a in the Supporting Information. The copper electrode was also treated under the same conditions for comparison purpose. Figure 1a and Figure S1a in the Supporting Information compare the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of the as-prepared CuCo650-400 with Cu-650-400 catalysts, respectively. From the images, roughened nanostructures can be observed clearly. Meanwhile, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images further show that the randomly dispersed nanowires of CuCo-650-400 with a diameter of about 50 nm can be found on the surface. The highly roughened surface can provide a large number of steps and edges as active sites for the electroreduction. A d-spacing of 0.209 nm is observed in the high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image (Figure 1b), which is assigned to the Cu (111) plane. By comparing Figure 1a and
Figure S1a in the Supporting Information, it can be observed that the addition of small amount of cobalt on the surface has limited influence to the morphology of the Cu-based electrocatalysts. In Figure 1d,e, the morphology of these samples changes slightly after reduction, which further proves the catalysts a decent structural stability. Therefore, the gas atmosphere treatment enhances the stability of the catalysts.
The samples were also characterized with X-ray diffraction (XRD). Figure 2a shows the patterns of as-prepared Cu-650400 and CuCo-650-400 catalysts and their patterns after CO2 electroreduction. It should be noted that only Cu can be observed since the amount of Co deposited to Cu is too less to be observed from the XRD patterns, though the existence of Co can be observed from energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping (Figure 1c,f). Peaks value at 43.3°, 50.4°, 68.0°, and 74.1° can be indexed to the diffraction of (111), (200), (220) planes of Cu with a face-centered cubic (fcc) structure, matching with the standard card of Cu (Joint Committee on Powder Diffraction Standards (JCPDS) Card No. 70-3039), which indicates the complete reduction of oxidized Cu or Co-modified Cu electrodes to metallic electrodes. The Cu (200) lattice plane intensity decreased after electrolysis reactions for both Cu and Co modified Cu electrodes. Moreover, Figure 2b shows the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectra of a) Cu 2p and b) Co 2p of all samples. The existence of Co can be observed from the Co 2p XPS spectra on CuCo and CuCo-650. However, it should be noticed that the surface enrichment of Cu through surface segregation is induced by heat treatment, because the surface energy of Cu is lower than that of Co.[4,25] Consequently, the Co concentration on the surface of CuCo-650-400 is too low to be detected by XPS, although the EDS mapping demonstrates the existence of Co in CuCo-650-400. Meanwhile, the ratio of Cu and Co of CuCo-650-400 is measured to be ≈50:1 by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. This result also indicates the existence of Co. In addition, the XRD and XPS spectra can again prove the reduction of the oxidized Co-modified Cu electrode into the metallic electrode before the CO2 electrolysis, as the Cu2+ satellite peaks disappear after the electroreduction treatment. The negligible peaks attributed to Cu(OH)2 and CuO are due to the oxidation of Cu at ambient conditions.[24]
The surface roughness factors of as-prepared Cu-650-400 and CuCo-650-400 electrodes are first estimated based on the double layer capacitance in 0.1 m KHCO3 solution at 0.3 V in

the range of 0.25 to 0.35 V (shown in Figure S2, Supporting Information). The cobalt deposition led to a slight increase in capacitance to 2.02 × 10−3 F cm−2, compared to the value of 1.83 × 10−3 F cm−2 for Cu-650-400. The slight increase of the double layer capacitance indicates the increase of surface roughness, which should be ascribed to the cobalt deposition. As a result, in addition to the electronic effect after cobalt deposition, the increment in roughness of the electrode should also be considered accountable for the improved reactivity of CO2 electrochemical reduction (higher current density by electrode surface area). To evaluate the reactivity of different electrodes toward CO2 electroreduction, cyclic voltammetry was performed in 0.1 m KHCO3 electrolyte saturated with CO2 (shown in Figure S3, Supporting Information). The CuCo-650-400 electrode shows the highest reactivity toward CO2 electroreduction, and electrode with Ar and air treatment show significantly improved current densities compared to catalysts with only Ar treatment or no treatment.

The chronoamperometry of CO2 electroreduction was performed in CO2-saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 solution for 1 h. Figure 3a shows the Faradaic efficiencies of products from CO2 electroreduction catalyzed by the CuCo-650-400 electrode at applied potential ranging from −0.45 V to −0.85 V. The CuCo-650-400 electrode exhibits a volcano-shape relationship of the formic acid selectivity with the potential applied, whereas the yielding of hydrogen and carbon monoxide can be suppressed: 25% formic
Small Methods 2019, 1900362
© 2019 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim1900362 (5 of 7)
acid FE at −0.45 V, the highest formic acid FE of around 80% at −0.65 V, and a formic acid FE value of 50% at −0.85 V.
The influence of heat treatment was then evaluated. Figure 3c further compares current densities of formic acid from CO2 reduction on Cu-650, Cu-650-400, CuCo-400, and CuCo-650-400 electrodes. The CuCo-650-400 electrode exhibits the largest formic acid current densities, which is likely to be a result of the effective roughened surface and the change in electronic structure. In Figure 3d, the Cu-650 electrode shows a formic acid FE of 25% at −0.45 V, which increases monotonically to 40% at −0.85 V. The trend of formic acid yielding is the same but slightly lower when compared to a value of 45% FE at −0.8 V reported before by the oxide-derived copper electrode.[18] The Cu-650-400 electrode prepared by further air heat treatment exhibits a formic acid FE of 20% at −0.45 V, which increases to 57% FE at −0.65 V, and then declines to 30% FE at −0.85 V. The formic acid current density of Cu-650-400 is higher than that of Cu-650, as a result of the roughened surface brought by the air treatment. Meanwhile, the formic acid current density and FE (at −0.65 V) of Cu-650-400 electrode are lower than those of CuCo-650-400 electrode, mainly due to the change in the electronic structure. Comparatively, the CuCo-400 electrode exhibit a formic acid FE of 20% at −0.45 V, an FE value of 57% at −0.65 V, and a decreased value of 30% at −0.85 V. From the abovementioned FE values at −0.65 V, the formic acid FE of 56% for Cu-650-400 electrode is nearly the same with that of CuCo-400 electrode, but much smaller than that of CuCo-650-400 electrode. This result indicates that the surface segregation by Ar atmosphere treatment procedure is a crucial factor in promoting the activity and selectivity of catalysis toward HCOOH.
To evaluate the influence of the amount of Co deposited and roughened surface brought by air atmosphere treatment on the selectivity of carbon dioxide reduction to formic acid, the electrodes were prepared with different amounts of Co deposited on Cu foil, ranging from 0.008 C to 0.065 C cm−2 with deposition periods from 1 to 240 s at −0.9 V versus saturated calomel electrode, which equal to cobalt surface densities of 0.04–0.34 µmol cm−2. After deposition, the electrodes directly
used are nominated as CuCo-ns (Co deposition time: n = 1, 3, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 240 s), while electrodes further treated with Ar atmosphere were nominated as CuCo-650-ns (Co deposition time: n = 1, 3, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 240 s), and the electrodes treat with Ar and air atmosphere were nominated as CuCo650-400-ns (Co deposition time: n = 1, 3, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 240 s). Figure S4a in the Supporting Information shows the CuCo-ns electrode directly used after Co deposition onto the Cu foil, which greatly enhances the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER): only hydrogen can be detected in the gas phase, and no liquid phase product can be observed. Figure S4b in the Supporting Information shows that after treated with Ar atmosphere, the CuCo-650-ns electrode yields low amount of formic acid (no more than 20% formic acid FE) when the totally deposited Co is below 0.04 µmol cm−2. The formic acid FE of decreases dramatically to only 3% when the deposition time is prolonged to 30 s, and only hydrogen can be detected when higher amount of Co is deposited. However, the formic acid selectivity is improved to the highest value of ≈80% at deposition time of 60 s (equals to the Co deposition amount of 0.12 μmol cm−2) after further treatment with air atmosphere (shown in Figure 4). After the systematic optimization of Co deposition amount and heat treatment conditions, both the highest FE and current density of formic acid are achieved by CuCo-650-400 electrode, at −0.65 and −0.85 V, respectively. These results suggest the CuCo-650-400 electrode the optimal of all electrodes studied in this work.
The experimental results show that CuCo-650-400 can catalyze the carbon dioxide electroreduction to yield formic acid, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen. Evidences indicate the volcano type FE distributions for formic acid with deposition amount of cobalt and overpotential applied. A possible explanation is as follow: the CO2/HCOO− reaction can be dominant with suitable amount of deposited cobalt, as there may be synergistic influence of both morphology change and electronic effect, especially with surface segregation induced by heat treatment.[25] When higher amount of cobalt is deposited, or the applied potential is at lower CO2/HCOO− overpotential regions, the HER is dominant since it is both thermodynamic and kinetic more favorable.[26–28]
Small Methods 2019, 1900362
© 2019 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim1900362 (6 of 7)
While when the applied potential is at higher CO2/HCOO− overpotential regions, the HER reaction regains its dominance as the mass transport of CO2 is limited due to the poor solubility of CO2 in aqueous electrolyte. Based on factors mentioned above, a possible mechanism considering the electronic effect of cobalt can be proposed. Two pathways (shown in Scheme S1, Supporting Information) can be summarized for the formation of formic acid: one is the formation of COOH* (carbon coordination) with an overpotential of −0.41 V, which can be regarded as initial step and will convert into CO*, a key intermediate responsible for the formation of other hydrocarbon products, such as CO, CH4, C2H4, CH3OH, etc.; the other pathway proposed is the formation of HCOO* (oxygen coordination) with an overpotential of −0.61 V, and this will be responsible in some reactions requiring more negative overpotential. Both intermediates can undergo reduction and form formic acid.[29,30] In this work, the yielding of formic acid is greatly enhanced after the coating of Co and follow-up heat treatment, while the ratio of formic acid to CO does not change significantly. In addition, Figure S3f in the Supporting Information demonstrates the Tafel slopes using formate partial currents. The Tafel slopes of the CuCo-650-400 and Cu-650-400 electrodes are 192 and 283 mV dec−1, respectively. These slopes suggest that the rate-determining step is the initial single electron transfer to CO2 to form CO2− intermediate, meanwhile a diffusion limitation may also influence the investigated electrodes.[31–33] Therefore, a possible explanation is that the as-prepared CuCo catalyst facilitate the formation of COOH* and/or HCOO* intermediates, while the HER is not facilitated or even hindered. To support this hypothesis, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were then employed to better understand the improved formic acid selectivity on the CuCo-650-400 catalysts. Figure 5 compares the energetics of adsorbed CO2 protonation to form COOH* and HCOO* on the (111) facet of Cu or CuCo at 0 V versus RHE. It can be seen that both routes to form COOH* and HCOO* are more favorable on CuCo compared with on Cu. In addition, the DFT calculations also suggest that the HER activities are almost the same on Cu and CuCo catalysts (shown in Figure S5, Supporting Information). These results suggest that the formation of COOH*/HCOO* is more favorable compared with H2 when catalyzed by the CuCo catalyst, and the higher formic acid selectivity is achieved as a result. In summary, an oxide-derived cobalt-decorated copper thin film catalyst with improved activity and selectivity was fabricated via the electrodeposition and followed with Ar and air atmosphere treatment. The high-performance liquid chromatography
Small Methods 2019, 1900362
© 2019 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim1900362 (7 of 7)
(HPLC) analysis of the liquid phase products of the as-prepared CuCo catalyst suggests a formic acid selectivity from carbon dioxide reduction dependent on the amount of deposited cobalt. The bimetallic catalyst with optimal deposition time exhibits decent selectivity and efficiency toward formic acid and diminished HER at the same time, when suitable potential is selected. However, the results also show that excess amount of cobalt deposition promotes the HER. The results also show the importance of Ar and air atmosphere treatment for the optimization of catalysts. The optimized CuCo bimetallic catalyst treated with Ar and air converts carbon dioxide to formic acid with an FE of ≈80% at −0.65 V versus RHE. Therefore, the reported cobaltdecorated copper catalysts for CO2 electroreduction in aqueous electrolyte are a potential technique for highly efficient, selective, and economic realization of the sustainable carbon cycle.
